name: Camellia japonica extract
lead: Camellia japonica extract is a botanical ingredient made from the Japanese camellia (tsubaki), an evergreen tree or shrub native to China and Japan. In skin care it is used for its reputed soothing and conditioning properties, and cosmetic formulas that include it are marketed for moisturising, skin-brightening and anti-ageing purposes [1][2][3]. Related seed oil from the same plant, known as tsubaki oil, is a traditional Japanese hair and skin oil [5].

The leaves are rich in anti-inflammatory terpenoids such as lupeol and squalene and can be made into a tea containing caffeine and catechins similar to those in the tea plant [1]. Korean patent filings from 2004 and 2005 describe cosmetic compositions of the extract aimed at skin ageing, whitening and inflammation [2][3]. A 2025 study in hairless mice reported that topical extract reduced atopic-dermatitis-like signs [4]. No human studies were found.

paras: Camellia japonica is a tree or shrub usually 1.5 to 6 metres tall, with leathery dark green leaves 5 to 11 cm long and large rose or white flowers that open from January to March in the wild [1]. It is native to forests in China and Japan, and a variety called yuki-tsubaki (snow camellia) grows in heavy-snow areas of northern Honshu [1]. In Japanese literature the early-spring flower is a symbol of resilience and modest beauty [1].

Extracts for cosmetics are made from leaves, flowers or seeds. One Korean patent filing describes a supercritical extract stabilised in nanoliposomes at 0.1 to 20 percent of a cosmetic composition to preserve skin from ageing, brighten skin and improve moisture and elasticity [2]. A second filing describes an extract with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity for cosmetic use [3].

Camellia japonica (Japanese tsubaki) is the main source of tea-seed oil in Japan, where it is used for hair, cosmetic and pharmaceutical purposes rather than mainly for cooking, and it is listed in the Japanese Pharmacopoeia as a fatty oil from the seeds [5]. Oil from the Goto and Izu Islands is described as especially prized for purity [5]. Camellia seed oils from related species, such as Camellia oleifera, are rich in oleic acid, with a profile similar to olive oil [5]. The oil is also traditionally used to protect Japanese swords from rust [5].

Camellia oleifera by-products and oil have been the subject of review articles describing anti-inflammatory and antioxidant constituents such as squalene, tea polyphenols and saponins [6][7]; these concern a related species and the seed oil rather than Camellia japonica leaf extract.

In the 2025 mouse study, hairless SKH-1 mice with chemically induced atopic dermatitis received topical Camellia japonica extract for four weeks. The treatment reduced epidermal thickness, mast cell infiltration and overall atopic-dermatitis-like symptoms [4]. The patent filings claim moisturising, whitening and elasticity effects but are not clinical evidence [2][3].
No studies found. Related animal and laboratory research is limited to the 2025 mouse model of atopic dermatitis [4].

card.summary: Japanese camellia botanical used in some cosmetics, with one mouse study and no human data.
card.note: Only animal and patent material found.

quick.overview:
An extract from the Japanese camellia shrub, used in some cosmetics.
The only published research is a 2025 mouse study; no human studies exist.
quick.mechanism: In mice, topical extract reduced skin inflammation markers in an atopic dermatitis model.
quick.risks: No safety data for human cosmetic use were found.
